gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1002r:
Radiation Exposure Compensation Act: Program Status, GAO-05-1002R of September 28, 2005, tracks a federal pay plan for people harmed by Cold War atomic tests. The United States ran above-ground tests from 1945 through 1962. The act, passed on October 15, 1990, set up partial pay for victims who later fell ill. The Justice Department began to handle claims in April 1992.

GAO checks the fund's cash, the count of claims won, lost, and pending, and how long each claim takes. It also adds up the pay given so far. A past GAO warning drives the review: the trust fund may run short of the cash that valid claims will need.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1032r:
Federally Chartered Corporation, GAO-05-1032R of September 30, 2005, is a short audit letter on the National Conference on Citizenship. The group holds a federal charter and works to promote citizenship across the United States. By law, such groups must file yearly audit reports with Congress. GAO reads those audits and reports what it finds.

The letter covers the group's books for fiscal years 2003 and 2002. Outside auditors said the books were fairly shown under standard accounting rules. GAO found no case of rule-breaking worth a report. The clean result, and the audit path behind it, make up the whole text.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-402r:
Payment Processing, GAO-05-402R of March 31, 2005, is a letter that gives GAO's view on a plan to pay move bills by wire. The Pentagon's Families First plan would reshape how troops' home goods are hauled. The Army asked if the plan's steps for wire bills and pay meet GAO's own book of proof rules for such pay. A finance arm had urged that the view be sought.

GAO tests the plan, as drawn on paper, next to the proof rules in its guide. It ran no tests on a live tool and took the plan's facts as given. Its view tells the Pentagon what proof each wire pay must hold.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-492r:
Whether NASA stayed within legal cost caps for the space station is the question in a GAO letter, GAO-05-492R, sent on April 8, 2005. The NASA Authorization Act of 2000 capped station development spending at $25 billion. It capped shuttle launch support at $17.7 billion. The act requires GAO to verify the amounts NASA charges against those caps. Enclosed briefing slides sum up the check.

NASA reported that about $23.5 billion of the $23.7 billion provided for the station from fiscal year 1994 through 2004 had been spent by September 30, 2004. It did not report shuttle launch costs at all. Once again, NASA could not give detailed support for its figures. GAO therefore could not verify the amounts in budget requests for fiscal years 2002 through 2006. NASA had put a new finance system in place to fix its data problems. Big start-up troubles with that system remained. The letter records a cap that could not be checked.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-502r:
GAO letter GAO-05-502R, sent June 10, 2005, covers the Fleet Reserve Association and the audits of its fiscal years ended December 31, 2003, and 2002. The association helps members and their families who face urgent need. It aids recruiting for the Navy, Marine Corps, and Coast Guard. It also keeps members up to date on matters of those services.

The charter law lays three duties on such groups. They must give a full picture of assets and debts in yearly statements. They must have an independent audit each year. They must send the auditor's report and statements to Congress. GAO read the papers and checked the figures in a limited way. Its goal was to warn the House Judiciary Committee of any lapse. It found none worth reporting. The auditors judged the statements fairly presented under generally accepted accounting principles.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-512r:
The National Academy of Public Administration is the chartered corporation in GAO letter GAO-05-512R, dated June 10, 2005. The academy gives independent advice on how government is organized and run. It counsels on public processes and programs. The letter covers the audit report for its fiscal year ended September 30, 2003.

Under title 36, the academy must present yearly financial statements and have them audited by an independent accountant. GAO was asked to read the audit report and warn the House Judiciary Committee of any reporting fault. Staff read the statements and notes and applied analytical procedures to the figures. No fault with the law's reporting requirements was identified. The auditor's opinion held that the statements were fairly presented under United States generally accepted accounting principles. GAO did not perform an audit.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-592r:
For the Department of State, GAO's findings on its fiscal year 2004 representation letter appear in GAO-05-592R, a report of June 23, 2005. The department's letter is one of many that underpin the audit of the U.S. government's financial statements. GAO reviewed five key areas. Three of them fell short of what the audit manual expects from such letters.

The department did not state the materiality thresholds it used. Its letter held 24 of the 29 standard representations that applied. Of the other 5, 3 were partial and 2 were missing. A summary of uncorrected errors was also incomplete. It gave no account of the errors, and it did not separate errors in dealings with other agencies from errors in dealings with the public. GAO made three recommendations to the acting chief financial officer. It also called on the inspector general to help ensure complete letters in future years.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-602r:
The Justice Department's fiscal year 2004 representation letter is the subject of GAO letter GAO-05-602R, sent on July 22, 2005. The letter confirms the department's figures for the audit of the government's financial statements. GAO reviewed five key areas. It found two that needed improvement before future letters can fully support the government-wide audit.

The letter included 28 of the 29 standard representations that applied to the department. The one remaining representation was not provided at all. The finance chief later addressed that omission in comments on the draft. The second fault was the error summary. The list of uncorrected misstatements was incomplete, and it offered no description of the misstatements. GAO made two recommendations to the chief financial officer. The inspector general was asked to work with the department and its outside auditors on future letters. Both offices said they will address the conditions noted.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-682r:
Lightning safety for federal buildings is surveyed in GAO letter GAO-05-682R, sent May 19, 2005. Four agencies holding over 80 percent of government space were studied. All four use the national standard, NFPA-780, for fitting protection systems, and its risk method to decide which buildings need them. None of the four gathers data on lightning damage or its costs.

Officials in strike-prone regions told GAO lightning is not a major worry, since they trust the gear in place. The letter weighs whether one uniform federal rule is needed and finds practice already largely aligned. All four agencies agreed with the findings.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-752r:
The Navy's next destroyer is tracked in letter GAO-05-752R, dated June 14, 2005. The ship is built to strike targets ashore and to rule shallow coastal waters. To cut risk, the Navy built 10 test models of key subsystems. The models cover the ship's 12 new technologies. GAO focused this update on five of the ten models.

An earlier GAO report had warned that the schedule left too little time to learn before key choices. Some test models were on plan then. Others faced hard technical problems. The letter reports what fresh tests and design reviews show for the five models. It gives readers a check on whether the test-first approach is paying off.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-812r:
Poor performers in the federal workplace frame GAO-05-812R, a letter dated June 29, 2005. Good performance systems link each worker's results to the agency's goals. They also help managers reward top staff and deal with weak staff. The letter weighs new personnel rules at the Homeland Security department. Those rules set up a modern pay system.

GAO found the rules hold many sound principles. Pay bands and job clusters that reflect labor markets are part of the design. But the rules are an outline, not a full plan. Much detail still must be written. Staff and unions are to help shape that detail. They hold four seats on the pay committee. GAO said lasting, committed leadership will be key.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-932r:
U.S. help for Iraq's January 2005 elections is reported in GAO-05-932R, a letter dated September 7, 2005. The vote chose a transitional national assembly on January 30, 2005. Power had passed to an Iraqi interim government on June 28, 2004. The United States obligated about $130 million to help prepare. The money aided the election commission, civic groups, and political bodies.

Much of the aid also aimed at two later votes set for 2005: a constitutional referendum and a further election. GAO gathered the facts as part of its wider watch on Iraq rebuilding. The letter records who got help and for what. It gives Congress a compact account of how the election support was spent. The work ran under the Comptroller General's own authority.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-962r:
Nuclear force spending under the New Triad is revisited in GAO-05-962R, a letter dated August 4, 2005. GAO reported in June 2005 on how the Defense Department counts and plans New Triad spending. That report urged clearer naming of projected spending. It also urged a long-term investment approach. The department's comments came too late for the June report. This letter presents them.

The letter sums up the June report's aims, findings, and recommendations. It then gives the department's comments in full. GAO's evaluation of those comments follows. Readers can see where the department agrees, where it pushes back, and whether GAO holds its line. The exchange keeps the spending visibility dispute on the public record. It also frames what Congress can press for next on long-term nuclear investment.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1002r:
Cost accounting practice at two departments is surveyed in GAO-06-1002R, a letter dated September 21, 2006. Laws and standards have long pushed agencies to know their costs. A 1990 law tells finance chiefs to build systems that report cost data. A federal standard sets the concepts for such accounting. A 1996 law built on that base. Congress asked GAO how far agencies in fact develop cost information.

This letter covers two departments: Agriculture and Housing and Urban Development. It tests their practice against the laws, standards, and system rules in force. Readers can see what cost data each department builds and where it falls short. The letter is one piece of a wider GAO check on whether the government's cost accounting push has taken hold in daily management.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1062r:
Aid screening in the West Bank and Gaza is reviewed in GAO-06-1062R, a letter dated September 29, 2006. The United States gave over $2 billion in aid there from fiscal years 1993 through 2005. Nearly $275 million came in fiscal year 2005 alone. Rules aim to keep aid from supporting terrorist acts. GAO checked how the aid mission vets people and certifies awards.

GAO found limits in how the mission ran its antiterrorism checks for fiscal year 2005 awards. Until June 2006, it did not routinely gather birth dates and places, or verify names given by awardees. About 94 percent of vetting memos said more identifying data was needed for a full check. In March 2006, the mission dropped periodic rechecks for some awardees. In its comments, it agreed to restore them. Many flaws are being fixed, GAO found, but more work is urged.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-122r:
Haitian immigration cases are counted in GAO-06-122R, a letter report dated October 21, 2005. The Haitian Refugee Immigration Fairness Act of 1998 let certain Haitian nationals seek lawful permanent residence. The law orders the Comptroller General to report every six months. Each report counts how many Haitians applied and how many were approved. This is the thirteenth report in that series. Reports continue until every application is finally decided.

The counts break applicants into the groups the law names. They cover asylum applicants, parolees, children without parents, orphaned children, and abandoned children. Eligible dependents, such as spouses and children, are counted as well. The report draws figures from the citizenship and immigration agency and from the immigration courts. It sorts applications received from those approved by each body. The letter is a running public ledger for a single relief law.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-172r:
Garage door openers knocked out by military radios are the odd but real topic of GAO-06-172R, a letter report dated December 1, 2005. The Defense Department is fielding new land mobile radios at bases nationwide. The radios run from 380 to 399.9 megahertz. Unlicensed garage door openers have used that same band for years. Near some bases, openers began to fail as the radios spread. Congress asked GAO to size the problem and review the department's development and outreach work.

The law favors the military here. Garage openers are unlicensed devices, so they must accept interference from licensed users. GAO reviewed what the department did as it built and tested the radios. It also studied plans to work with the towns affected. GAO urged the Secretary of Defense to put the outreach plans in writing and affirm them. The department agreed and said it would follow through.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-212r:
How the airwaves get divided is introduced in GAO-06-212R, a letter report dated November 10, 2005. The radio spectrum carries mobile phones, broadcasts, radar, and satellite links. It is a scarce natural resource vital to the economy and to security. Two bodies manage it. The Federal Communications Commission handles nonfederal users, while a Commerce Department agency handles federal users. They allocate bands to types of service, then assign licenses to users. The aim is to keep signals from clashing.

Demand for spectrum has exploded as new wireless services reach the market. Public safety users need more room too, above all after disasters. Nearly every party now presses for a larger share. This letter gives early facts on how allocation and assignment work. It sets the stage for later GAO work on a crowded resource. Readers new to spectrum policy get a clear primer here.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-222r:
Understated cost growth on a spy drone is exposed in GAO-06-222R, a letter report dated December 15, 2005. Law requires the Defense Department to tell Congress when a program's unit cost jumps past set marks. At a 25 percent breach, the Secretary must certify the program as vital, with no cheaper equal option. In April 2005 the Air Force reported an 18 percent rise for the Global Hawk drone. GAO was already reviewing drone buying plans. It paused to check the Air Force figures and found them wanting.

Key retrofit costs were left out of the report, GAO found. Back in, they lift the rise to 22.5 percent over the baseline. The department partly agreed with GAO's call to fix the report. It accepted that the sensor retrofit costs belonged in the count. GAO urged full compliance with the cost reporting law. Congress can only police growth it can see.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-292r:
A census of federal benefit programs that test applicants' finances is delivered in GAO-06-292R, a letter dated December 14, 2005. Bad data from applicants helps drive billions in improper payments each year. Agencies need trustworthy personal and financial facts to judge who qualifies. The tax agency holds one of the largest stores of such data in the country. Congress asked GAO to gather this picture as part of wider work on verifying finances.

The letter lists the federal benefit programs that carry a financial eligibility test. For each, it states what papers an applicant must show to qualify. The aim is a shared map for lawmakers weighing data checks. Better checks promise fewer payments to people who do not qualify. They also raise questions about privacy and burden on honest applicants. The letter keeps to facts and lets the policy debate follow.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-302r:
Follow-up answers on the FBI's technology management fill GAO-06-302R, a letter dated December 21, 2005. The letter answers questions left from GAO's testimony of September 14, 2005. That testimony judged the bureau's progress in building the management skill to modernize its systems. A new case management system sits at the center of the effort. System upgrades form a key part of the bureau's reinvention after the September 11 attacks. Lawmakers pressed for detail in writing.

The replies walk through management practices and the case system purchase. They record what the bureau had done and what remained weak. Written answers lock an agency to its claims in a way hearings cannot. The letter is thus both evidence and pledge. It captures a watchdog and a bureau mid-argument about competence. Readers can track each promise against later reports on the same troubled program.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-522r:
The office that manages the national debt must keep its computer controls tight. Letter GAO-06-522R, dated March 16, 2006, reports on information security at the Bureau of the Public Debt. The work supports GAO's audit of the federal government's statements. GAO audited the schedules of federal debt for fiscal years ended September 30, 2005 and 2004. As part of that work, it tested security controls over key bureau systems.

GAO reviewed general and application controls. It followed up on fixes for flaws found in prior audits. It also assessed systems run for the bureau by Federal Reserve Banks. Areas for improvement were identified. A separate report covers the Reserve Banks' results.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-582r:
Written answers after a hearing can carry as much weight as spoken ones. Letter GAO-06-582R, dated March 24, 2006, collects post-hearing questions on the Defense Department's National Security Personnel System. On November 17, 2005, the Comptroller General testified before a Senate panel. The hearing weighed proposed and final rules for the new personnel system. Senators then sent questions for the record. This letter holds the responses.

The answers cover labor relations for unique parts of the workforce. They also cover employee involvement, system evaluation, and effects on veterans. Other topics include teamwork, fairness, pay and performance standards, and safeguards against abuse. Readers get GAO's positions in direct question-and-answer form.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-772r:
Internal controls at the deposit insurance agency are the subject of GAO-06-772R, a management report dated July 11, 2006. GAO found the issues while auditing the 2005 financial statements of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation. The corporation runs funds that insure bank deposits and pay for bank supervision. Control flaws in its own accounting can erode trust in those funds. This report collects the problems GAO judged worthy of management attention.

GAO identified several internal control issues that touched the accounting for the funds the corporation administers. The flaws did not overturn the audit results, but they raised risk. GAO made eight recommendations for strengthening internal controls and accounting procedures. The audits followed government auditing standards. The report gives the agency a concrete fix list for its back office.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-912r:
Past GAO findings on farm lending are gathered in GAO letter GAO-06-912R, dated June 28, 2006. Congress asked for the summary ahead of a June 13, 2006 hearing on farm loan programs at the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

The letter pulls together GAO work from the 1990s through 2002 on USDA lending practice. It adds GAO views on how the loan programs then stood and how they were run. It closes with points Congress should weigh. For readers, the value is the long view: one short letter that traces years of audit findings on farm credit, and what they imply for oversight now.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-922r:
Former Members of Congress, a federally chartered group, has its audit passed on in GAO letter GAO-06-922R, dated July 7, 2006. The group works to build public grasp of Congress and public support for it. Chartered groups must present audited accounts each year.

Coverage is the fiscal year that ended December 31, 2004. GAO read the audit report on the group's statements for that year. The auditor judged the statements fairly shown, in line with U.S. accounting rules. GAO noted no rule breach that called for a report. The letter is brief by design: a formal word to Congress that the yearly audit check is done.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-132r:
Airports and airways are funded in part by ticket and fuel excise taxes. GAO examined the bookkeeping behind those taxes in GAO-07-132R, issued November 3, 2006. The letter reports agreed-upon procedures for the Airport and Airway Trust Fund. The Transportation Department agreed to the scope of the work. It covers the fiscal year ended September 30, 2006. The aim was to see whether net tax revenue sent to the fund was supported by the records.

GAO tested transactions that underlie the amounts distributed to the fund. It reviewed the tax agency's quarterly certifications and Treasury's adjustments during the year. It also checked estimates used for the fourth quarter distribution. Key reconciliations tied tax agency records to Treasury records. As with its sister letters, GAO makes no claim that the agreed procedures were sufficient. The enclosure pairs each procedure with its findings.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-142r:
NASA buys goods and services around the world, not just at home. A GAO letter, GAO-07-142R, dated November 9, 2006, checked how the agency tracks that foreign buying. A 2005 law requires NASA to report yearly on contracts performed overseas. The report must also list purchases open only to foreign sources. It must note where the Buy American Act was waived under trade deals. The first report was due in January 2007.

GAO found that NASA would not fully meet that first deadline. The agency relies on a governmentwide procurement database for its figures. That system does not track subcontracts or Buy American Act exceptions. So NASA lacked key data Congress asked for. GAO also found that NASA did not collect supplier base data across the whole agency. It had such data only for the Space Shuttle program. GAO made no recommendations, noting steps already under way.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-322r: Congress charters certain veterans and civic groups, and GAO checks their outside audits. GAO-07-322R, a letter dated January 26, 2007, covers the Legion of Valor of the United States of America, Inc. GAO reviewed the audit reports on its financial statements for fiscal years 2006 and 2005. The auditor found the statements presented fairly under U.S. accounting principles. GAO found no reportable instances of noncompliance.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-372r: The Pentagon's personnel data center feeds official counts of how officers earn their commissions, and those counts cannot be trusted. GAO raised the alarm in GAO-07-372R, a letter dated March 8, 2007. The center holds the military's largest archive of personnel data. Its figures feed the annual report on representation in the forces. GAO hit the reliability problems while preparing its January 19, 2007 report on officer accessions. The letter lays out the issues for defense officials. It pairs them with recommendations to correct the data.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-382r:
Passenger rail policy needs a national plan before more money can do much good. GAO made the case in GAO-07-382R, a letter dated January 18, 2007. The letter highlights GAO's November 13, 2006 report on intercity rail. Amtrak draws over $1 billion a year in federal support. Its losses stay high, and repair backlogs run to billions. Congress faces clashing visions for the service. Some want growth; others want cuts.

The current system is in poor financial shape, GAO found. Federal funds do not flow where public benefit is greatest. Foreign reforms offer three lessons. A nation must set clear policy goals first. It must assign roles to each level of government. It must lock in stable funding. The United States is poorly set to do any of the three. Views on rail's purpose diverge too widely. The letter urges a policy before structural choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-472r:
The Reserve Officers Association of the United States backs a strong defense policy, and its yearly audit is reviewed in GAO-07-472R, a GAO letter released March 9, 2007. The association is a federally chartered corporation. Its stated aim is to support a military policy that gives the nation sound security. Federal law requires the group to file full yearly financial statements and to obtain an outside audit.

GAO's letter covers the fiscal year ended March 31, 2005. Staff read the audit report and the statements behind it. They ran checks on the figures but did not audit the books or give their own opinion. The review found no reportable breach of the law's reporting rules. The auditors held that the statements were fairly presented under standard accounting rules. The letter is one of a set of charter reviews GAO sent that day.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-482r:
Bookkeeping flaws at the market watchdog are detailed in GAO-07-482R, a GAO report dated April 3, 2007. GAO audits the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) each year. Its audit of the fiscal year 2006 and 2005 statements came out on November 15, 2006. This follow-on report digs into the control flaws behind the numbers. It carries six fresh recommendations.

One gap was basic: for most furniture and gear tested, SEC could not show that staff matched what arrived against what was ordered. Sound proof turned up in only 10 of 49 cases. Payroll and personnel action handling also drew fire. GAO told SEC to judge whether its fixes work once they are fully in place. The report is a repair list for the office that polices other firms' books.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-492r:
Nurse aid may miss the hospitals that need it most, and GAO-07-492R, a GAO letter report of April 30, 2007, shows the flaw. Registered nurses form the largest group of U.S. health workers, with more than 2.4 million employed in 2004. A federal estimate put the nurse shortfall at about 111,000 in 2000. The Nurse Reinvestment Act of 2002 funds scholarships and loan repayment for nurses who serve 2 years at shortage sites.

The catch is the label itself. GAO found that the Health Resources and Services Administration lacked a sound way to tell which sites truly face a critical shortage. Awards could land where need is mild. A contractor study offered data and a method, still under review in March 2007. GAO told the health secretary to set steps and a time frame to adopt a proof-based method and to report progress each year.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-552r:
Bombing-range cleanup on Vieques is priced in GAO-07-552R, a GAO letter report dated March 26, 2007. The Navy fired live rounds on the island, off Puerto Rico, for decades. Training stopped in 2003. The land passed to the town of Vieques, a conservation trust, and the Department of the Interior. The Navy kept the duty to clean it up.

Two cleanup tracks run side by side. One handles hazardous substances at old sites. The other handles unexploded munitions and their residues. Congress asked GAO for the status of both and the cost to finish. The letter reports where work stands on each track. It gives the Navy's cost estimates for the years ahead. For island residents, the pace of that work decides when land is truly safe to use again.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-662r:
Body armor recalls and shortages are the subject of GAO-07-662R, a GAO letter report dated April 26, 2007. Since 2003, U.S. Central Command has required troops and Defense civilians in Iraq and Afghanistan to wear the Interceptor Body Armor system. The vest stops 9mm rounds; its plates stop 7.62mm armor-piercing rounds. Extra guards cover the shoulders, throat, and groin.

In May 2005, the Marine Corps recalled armor that missed contract terms. In November 2005, both services recalled 14 lots that failed ballistic tests. An April 2005 GAO report had already found shortages, traced to material and production limits and poor in-theater delivery. This letter checks what the Army and Marine Corps did next about fit, testing, and supply. Congress's stake is direct: the vest is the last line between a rifleman and the rounds aimed at him.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-692r:
GAO-07-692R, sent May 18, 2007, grades the Internal Revenue Service's first year under new control rules. The Office of Management and Budget's Circular No. A-123 tells agencies to test their own controls over financial reports. The rules bind 24 large finance agencies, Treasury among them. The IRS is a large part of Treasury. GAO checked whether the IRS planned its tests well in fiscal year 2006. It also checked the promise the IRS sent Treasury on its controls.

GAO found the IRS planned and ran its first-year review as the rules require. The work backed the promise the IRS sent Treasury as of June 30, 2006. GAO praised the agency's drive and care. Some gaps remained. Staff did not always write down the steps they took. Test results were not always tied clearly to the final judgments. GAO noted that full use of the rules will take years at an agency this size.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-72r:
Board independence at the National Credit Union Administration is covered in GAO-07-72R, a letter dated November 30, 2006. Public remarks by the agency's chairman had stirred doubts in Congress. The doubts touched the board's distance from the industry it polices. GAO compared the agency's controls with those at six other finance regulators. It weighed them against practices found in studies of good governance. It also checked the agency's use of a class of political staff.

All seven regulators share ethics rules and fixed board terms. Five of the six others add their own conflict rules, though. Some also stress independence in their mission statements. The credit union agency lacked those extra steps. Its board rules on who may serve matched the others, though. GAO found chances to strengthen the agency's governance frame. Clearer rules could guard the board's objectivity when it weighs industry data and pay.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-732r:
Controls over the Capitol Preservation Fund are faulted in GAO-07-732R, a report dated May 25, 2007. The Library of Congress runs money tasks for the fund. The fund serves the Capitol Preservation Commission. GAO audited the fund's fiscal years 2005 and 2004 accounts. Its March 2007 audit report flagged weak controls. This report spells out those flaws in depth. It makes four recommendations to the Library.

Controls failed to ensure the fund kept enough cash at Treasury to cover payments. Controls over drafting and checking the fund's statements also fell short. GAO called the flaws reportable conditions, not material weaknesses. That means they matter but do not doom the accounts. The Library agreed its controls could improve. It listed steps it will take in reply. The fixes aim to guard payments and sharpen the fund's reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-882r:
Costs of reviewing medical devices are verified in GAO-07-882R, a letter dated June 25, 2007. The Food and Drug Administration judges devices from catheters to artificial hearts. A 2002 law lets it charge user fees for device applications. The agency reports each year on fees, costs, and staffing. Device makers pressed for finer cost detail. GAO checked the methods behind those reports. It asked whether they follow federal cost accounting standards.

The methods are consistent with those standards, GAO found. The agency names the units that do review work. It builds full costs for each unit, counting direct and shared costs. It splits costs among application types by reviews completed. Managers use judgment where costs span more than one type. Staffing for reviews has generally risen in recent years. The letter walks through each step of the method. It gives Congress a base to judge the fee program's books.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-942r:
Bookkeeping controls at the deposit insurer are faulted in GAO-07-942R, a letter dated June 27, 2007. GAO audits the Deposit Insurance Fund each year. Its 2006 audit gave clean opinions on the statements. Control flaws still surfaced during the work. Written steps for the monthly ledger closing were patchy. Supervisors reviewed key tasks too loosely. Errors in closing work could slip through unseen. One error hit the loss rates used for failure reserves.

Receivership data were wrongly left out of those rates, GAO found. The slip could distort the liability shown for bank failures. Checks arriving at a Dallas site lacked proper safeguards. None of the flaws counts as a material weakness. They still merit fixing, the letter says. GAO urged fuller written procedures for core tasks. It also urged tighter review habits. The corporation agreed with the recommendations. It promised to spell out the closing steps in detail.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-172r:
Drug cost savings in the military health system are reported in GAO letter GAO-08-172R, dated October 31, 2007. Pharmacy costs have long pressed the Defense Department. In fiscal year 2006, it filled 115 million prescriptions for about 6.5 million people. The bill came to about $6 billion. A single preferred drug list, set up in 2005, is one brake on that growth.

The letter weighs how far that list has cut costs. Makers offer rebates to win a place on the list. Drugs are judged on clinical value and cost within their class. GAO reports reduced pharmacy costs from the list and the rebates together.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-202r:
Highway tax receipts are traced in GAO letter GAO-08-202R of November 2, 2007. The Highway Trust Fund receives excise tax money for road programs. The transport department asked GAO to test whether the sums sent to the fund for fiscal year 2007 rest on sound records. The department agreed to the procedures in advance.

GAO checked the deals behind the tax distributions. It reviewed the tax agency's quarterly certifications of receipts. It also checked Treasury adjustments and the tax office's method for estimating receipts. The letter follows standard attestation rules. It notes that the requesting office bears the call on whether the checks suffice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-232r:
Handling of sensitive security data is mapped in GAO letter GAO-08-232R, dated November 30, 2007. Since the 2001 attacks, agencies must shield tender facts from foes yet share them with partners who need them. The transport security agency marks such material as sensitive security information. A 2007 funding law told the security department to revise its rules for the marks.

GAO reviewed how designations are made and lifted. The agency has set criteria and examples for the marks. Sister agencies have begun to adapt those guides to their own work. The letter shows a system still spreading across the department.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-242r:
A truck safety overhaul earns a planning pass in GAO letter GAO-08-242R, dated December 20, 2007. Crashes with large trucks and buses kill about 5,500 people a year. About 160,000 more are hurt. The fatality rate's long decline has leveled off. The motor carrier safety agency plans a new regime, called CSA 2010, to push it down again.

The plan would rate nearly all carriers, and later drivers, on a rolling basis. It would swap some costly probes for lighter touch interventions. Better data would spot risky firms sooner. Congress asked GAO to judge the build-out. GAO calls the framework for managing and testing the plan reasonable.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-382r:
Outsourcing the Capitol Power Plant is weighed in GAO letter GAO-08-382R, dated January 31, 2008. Run by the Architect of the Capitol, the plant heats and cools about 16 million square feet in 24 facilities. A $100.9 million expansion of its West Refrigeration Plant was due to finish in March 2008, and staffing levels had drawn concern for over a decade.

Plant officials said they had cut costs by burning more coal and speeding the expansion, which they expect to save over $2 million a year. But they lacked papers showing the full costs and gains of these steps, or how staffing would change. Staffing had barely moved in years, despite advice to cut it by more than one third. A draft reorganization plan ran to a single page, and cuts were on hold until the expansion was done.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-512r:
Highway planning and environmental review are covered in GAO letter GAO-08-512R, dated April 25, 2008. Federal law requires reviews that weigh harm to water, wildlife, and historic sites before road work proceeds. A 2005 law, SAFETEA-LU, pushed planners to bring environmental thinking into long-range plans earlier.

All six state transport departments and six metro planning groups GAO contacted are taking early steps, and four have issued plans that meet the new rules. Early input from resource agencies can flag problems while fixes are cheap. But those agencies lack staff and funds for planning work, and early help is not part of their mission. Groups with strong past ties to resource agencies are moving fastest. The letter shares what helps these partnerships form.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-602r:
Base growth funding is tracked in GAO letter GAO-08-602R, dated April 1, 2008. The 2005 base closure round will move over 123,000 personnel through more than 800 actions. Other shifts bring about 50,000 soldiers home from Europe and Korea and add 92,000 active duty troops. Twenty places face growth that strains nearby towns.

At the 11 installations GAO reviewed, covering over 85 percent of growth troops, the services received about $7.3 billion for fiscal years 2006 through 2008. Just under $6.4 billion more is still sought for the remaining work. Off-base roads are a pinch point: one Defense Access Road project has funding, four more worth just over $37.7 million await review, and states and towns plan just over $657 million of their own road work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-612r:
The military trains doctors through scholarship and aid programs that pay for medical school. In return, doctors owe years of active duty service. GAO-08-612R, dated April 1, 2008, looks at what happens when a doctor leaves early and owes the government money back, and how well that debt gets collected.

Very few doctors left early. From fiscal years 2003 through 2007, fewer than 1 percent of the 19,921 people in the two programs quit or skipped duty. Still, some payback cases took more than 5 years to reach a debt account. The services and the finance center each thought the other side made the first move to collect.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-62r:
Program managers run the buying of major weapons, but much that shapes their work sits outside their control. GAO said in 2005 that they need more power if they are to be held to account. GAO-08-62R, a letter dated November 9, 2007, reports what the Department of Defense has done since then.

The department now asks managers, their bosses, and the troops who will use the weapon to sign shared goal agreements. It also plans more training, a formal mentoring program, and forums where managers share lessons. GAO notes real accountability also needs top leaders to rank programs and fund the top ones first.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-642r:
Private firms run most Energy Department sites, and the department pays much of their workers' pension and health costs. Those promises add up to a large long-term bill. GAO-08-642R, a letter dated June 19, 2008, sets out how the department watches those costs across 43 site contracts.

For 2007, the department reported a net bill of $10.3 billion for health and other benefits after retirement, plus $69.5 million for pensions. Firms must compare their benefit costs with at least 15 like employers. If costs top 105 percent of the group, the department can demand a fix plan, though it had not always done so.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-792r:
Deep water oil leases from the late 1990s sit at the heart of a court fight over royalties. A 1995 law let the government waive royalties to spur drilling when prices were low. GAO-08-792R, a letter dated June 5, 2008, updates what missing price limits on some leases may cost.

Leases from 1998 and 1999 lack the price caps that end relief when prices soar. Oil has passed $100 a barrel since then. An April 2007 GAO report warned the gap would likely cost billions in lost royalties. A court ruling against the caps adds risk that past royalties could be repaid too. Exact sums turn on future prices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-902r:
Public-private partnerships at military repair depots are the subject of GAO-08-902R, a July 2008 letter to the armed services committees. Congress directed the Defense Department to report on partnerships at its Centers of Industrial and Technical Excellence, and GAO checked that report against the six elements Congress required. The partnerships pair depot skills with private firms to gain efficiency and access to capital.

GAO found the report incomplete. It answered all six elements on the surface, but it did not directly describe two of them. One was the steps for finishing partnership contract talks within 12 months of starting them. The other was the plans to expand core depot capabilities through partnerships. The letter's title adds that more detail would make the report more useful to Congress as it weighs the depot program.
